title: A Thousand Nikumbhas, One True Head
story:
The Yadavas had won their war, and while they were busy at their sports the demon Nikumbha found his chance. The garden of Bhanu's women's quarters was supposed to be unapproachable; that was precisely why it stood unguarded. Years before, Pradyumna, the son of Krishna, had carried off Prabhavati, the daughter of Nikumbha's brother Vajranabha, and the demon had never forgiven the insult. Now he slipped in, seized Bhanumati, the beautiful daughter of Bhanu, and was gone before the weeping could even begin.

When the lamentation reached the men's quarters, Vasudeva — Krishna's father — and the elder Ahuka rushed out in fury and found only an empty garden. They went straight to Krishna. He asked no questions and called no council: with his friend Arjuna beside him he mounted Garuda, his great winged carrier; he ordered Pradyumna, whose banner bore the makara, a creature of the sea, to follow in his chariot; and he set off in pursuit. They caught Nikumbha long before he could reach the city of Vajra and the safety of his kinsmen.

The fight that followed was stranger than any of them had expected. Nikumbha fought smiling, a heavy club in his right hand and the weeping Bhanumati in his left, and because of her no one could strike him. Krishna, Pradyumna and Arjuna could have killed the demon a dozen times over; none of them could bear to wound the maiden. Arjuna, the finest of archers, solved the riddle the way a skilled man handles a serpent coiled around a camel: he struck the serpent and left the camel alone. His arrows, thin as reeds, found the demon again and again without ever touching the girl.

Then Nikumbha changed the game, for illusion was his art. In a single breath he and the maiden vanished so completely that even his pursuers could not tell where they had gone. A yellow vulture crossed the sky, and Arjuna's arrows bit into it — the demon, transformed, was fleeing. The chase carried them across all seven continents, until at last Nikumbha dropped onto the summit of Mount Gokarna, on the bank of the river Chela Ganga — a mountain guarded by the power of Mahadeva, the great god Shiva, which no god, demon or ascetic could cross.

He had chosen well — but not well enough. Pradyumna, himself a master of illusion, slipped past the demon's guard and snatched Bhanumati away, while Krishna and Arjuna drove Nikumbha back with arrows until he fled from the northern slope of the mountain to the southern. With Krishna's permission Pradyumna carried the maiden home to Dwaraka and returned at once, to find Krishna and Arjuna waiting at the mouth of the cave where Nikumbha had vanished — the hidden entrance to Shatpura, the city of his demon kin.

All night the three kept watch there. At dawn the demon came out to fight. Arjuna's arrows from the Gandiva, his great bow, sealed the passage — but Nikumbha broke through them, seized his thorn-covered club, and struck Arjuna full on the head. Blood poured from the hero's mouth and he fell senseless; the master of illusions snatched him up and carried him off. And then, all at once, the earth and the sky were full of demons.

Thousands of Nikumbhas filled the heavens — on the earth and in the sky, in every direction, identical faces, identical clubs, identical smiles. Every eye saw a thousand demons. Krishna saw only one. With a sight older than the world and its illusions, he perceived the true form of the creator of illusions standing among his own echoes, and the discus left his hand and flew true. It cut off the head of the real Nikumbha — and in that instant every false Nikumbha dissolved like mist at sunrise. The demon who had filled the sky with himself was gone, and Arjuna, whom he had carried off, was free.

The gates of Shatpura stood open and empty behind them. Krishna gathered his friend up onto Garuda, and they turned toward Dwaraka — leaving behind a city whose master had been destroyed by the very illusion he had trusted.
reflection: The thousand Nikumbhas are defeated not by force but by perception: Krishna wins the moment he sees through the illusion to the single true form behind it. Notice too that the whole pursuit was shaped by compassion — the heroes refused to strike until the maiden could be spared, so the killing blow came only when the fight could be finished cleanly.
content_note: Mild battle violence: a hero is knocked unconscious and a demon is beheaded by the discus; described without graphic detail.
next_story_tease: But Nikumbha had a brother, and that brother had already begun to ask the universe for a gift that would threaten all three worlds.
hero_scene: Krishna, calm amid a sky filled with a thousand identical Nikumbhas, sends his discus flying toward the one true form of the demon while the unconscious Arjuna lies at his feet and the false forms begin to dissolve.
